images.title: 1.9 Detect outliers
images.insight: pm2_5 and pm10 are right-skewed with long upper tails, while temperature and humidity are roughly bell-shaped. The IQR outlier removal will trim only the extreme pollution spikes, preserving the informative mid-range.

images.title: 1.11 Verify outliers were removed
images.insight: The boxplots after the IQR cut confirm the extreme spikes are gone while the core and whiskers of each distribution stay intact. This protects the models from a handful of implausible readings without distorting normal variability.

images.title: 2.4 Feature distributions before scaling
images.insight: The pairplot before scaling shows PM2.5's right skew and its near-linear relationship with PM10. Distributions and scales differ enough across features that standardization is warranted before training.

images.title: 3.1 Site coverage and sample size per site
images.insight: Monitoring coverage is uneven — a few sites report almost daily while others leave long gaps. This imbalance motivates the project: sites with thin coverage are exactly where a predictive model adds value.

images.title: 3.2 Strength/direction of relationships, guides feature selection
images.insight: PM2.5 correlates strongly with PM10 (r ≈ 0.97) but only weakly with temperature (r ≈ −0.22) and humidity. PM10 therefore belongs in the feature set, while weather alone cannot explain most of the variation.

images.title: 3.3 Shape of each distribution, skewness, whether pm2_5 is right-skewed (typical for pollution data)
images.insight: PM2.5 is right-skewed with occasional tall spikes, temperature is near-normal, and humidity is left-skewed toward high values. These shapes justify log/robust handling in some features and scale-insensitive tree models later.

images.title: 3.4 Relationship between PM2.5 and PM10
images.insight: PM2.5 and PM10 move almost in lockstep (r ≈ 0.97), so PM10 is by far the strongest single predictor available. Their near-perfect co-movement reflects shared emission sources (combustion, dust).

images.title: 3.5 Weekday vs Weekend pollution
images.insight: Weekdays and weekends look nearly identical (traffic is heavy everywhere in Nairobi daily), so a weekend flag adds little signal on its own. The model still keeps it as a minor feature for calendar completeness.

images.title: 3.6 Which locations are most polluted
images.insight: The most polluted sites sit near major road corridors, where traffic emissions concentrate. The spread between the cleanest and dirtiest sites is modest, though, hinting that site identity explains less than history and weather.

images.title: 3.7 Geographic hotspots across Nairobi
images.insight: Pollution is spread city-wide rather than concentrated in a single hotspot, so site identity adds limited signal once other features are known. The choropleth still reveals clusters around industrial corridors.

images.title: 3.8 Whether heat correlates with pollution levels
images.insight: Hotter days tend to have lower PM2.5 (r ≈ −0.22) — pollution is driven more by the cooler, stable conditions of the cold dry season. This is the strongest pure-weather driver and matches Nairobi's Jun–Aug peak.

images.title: 3.9 Whether humidity correlates with pollution levels
images.insight: Humidity shows almost no linear link to PM2.5 (r ≈ −0.03), so its value is indirect — wet-season dynamics enter the model through seasonal features instead. Keeping it costs little and preserves interactions for tree models.

images.title: 3.10 Seasonal patterns: PM2.5 distribution by month
images.insight: PM2.5 climbs through the year and peaks in the June–August window — a clear seasonal signature. The boxplot's whiskers widen in those months too, meaning not just higher means but more variable (worse) days.

images.title: 3.10.1 Monthly average PM2.5 trend
images.insight: The month-on-month rise confirms PM2.5 peaks mid-year and eases toward December. Season is therefore engineered as sin/cos features so the model can exploit the full yearly cycle, not just a month id.

images.title: 3.11.1 Apply categorization to the dataset
images.insight: The vast majority of readings fall into the Moderate band, so the classifier starts with a heavy class imbalance (Moderate ≈ 12,755 vs ~1,250 each for Good and Unhealthy). Accuracy alone would hide failures on the rare classes.

images.title: 3.12.1 Visualize class balance after SMOTE
images.insight: After SMOTE every class is represented by 12,755 training rows instead of being dominated by Moderate. A classifier trained on these balanced data can now learn Good/Unhealthy patterns instead of defaulting to the majority.

images.title: 5.3.2.1 Tune Ridge alpha (GridSearchCV)
images.insight: The validation curve shows a wide plateau, so the exact alpha matters little once regularization is in effect. The tuned alpha was still stored for the final Ridge model.

images.title: 5.3.6 Regression model comparison chart
images.insight: Random Forest wins across all three panels — lower RMSE/MAE and the highest R² of the four regressors. The linear models cluster together, and the polynomial adds a marginal step, so the winner's lead is decisive.

images.title: 5.4.4 Accuracy vs Macro-F1 (bar chart)
images.insight: Random Forest leads on both accuracy and macro-F1, so it earns the classification win on both metrics. Logistic Regression's lower macro-F1 signals that its accuracy is inflated by the majority class.

images.title: 5.4.5 Per-class precision/recall/F1 (grouped bars)
images.insight: The gap is widest on Good and Unhealthy: Logistic Regression lags recall there while Random Forest holds up. These are the classes that matter for health alerts, so the difference is consequential.

images.title: 5.4.6 ROC curves (one-vs-rest)
images.insight: Random Forest's one-vs-rest curves dominate Logistic Regression's on every class, and the advantage is biggest at low false-positive rates. That means RF flags true pollution episodes earlier with fewer false alarms.

images.title: 5.5.1 Class counts before vs after SMOTE (bar chart)
images.insight: The before/after bars make the rebalancing obvious — the classifier can no longer just predict Moderate everywhere. The balanced class counts are the direct cause of the recall gains on Good and Unhealthy.

images.title: 6.1 Learning curves (train vs cross-validated score by training size)
images.insight: The gap is small and flat past ~60% of the data, signaling the classifier has nearly converged. Adding data yields little here — the ceiling is set by feature quality and intrinsic noise, not sample size.

images.title: 6.1 Learning curves (train vs cross-validated score by training size)
images.insight: The two curves are close and still rising — a little more data (or more sites) would buy further accuracy. The absence of a wide train–CV gap also means the regressor is not overfitting at current sizes.

images.title: 6.2 Regression diagnostics — actual vs predicted, residuals
images.insight: Residuals spread widens at higher PM2.5, i.e., the model under-predicts the heaviest pollution days. The actual-vs-predicted scatter hugs the diagonal for typical days while the tail drifts below it.

images.title: 6.3 Classification diagnostics — confusion matrices
images.insight: SMOTE moves errors off the rare classes: false negatives drop for Good and Unhealthy with no big loss on Moderate. The confusion matrices show the balanced model trades a few Moderate misses for far fewer critical ones.

images.title: 6.4 Feature importance (both winning Random Forest models)
images.insight: The same trio — pm10, the 7-day mean, and yesterday's PM2.5 — dominates both tasks, so lagged history is the backbone of both models. Temperature and month features trail, confirming seasonality in second place.

images.title: 7.1 Permutation importance (both winning models)
images.insight: The classifier also leans hardest on physical PM readings rather than weather or site code, confirming history-first reasoning. The permutation ranking is reassuringly consistent with the feature-importance analysis.

images.title: 7.1 Permutation importance (both winning models)
images.insight: Shuffling pm10 and the 7-day PM2.5 mean costs the most R², matching the tree-based importance and confirming a history-first view. Weather and site features drop only a few points when permuted.

images.title: 7.2 Partial dependence plots (top features)
images.insight: Every top-feature curve rises monotonically — more PM10, a longer high streak, or warmer 7-day temperatures all push predicted PM2.5 up. The curves are smooth with modest slopes, indicating stable, interpretable responses.

texts.title: 1.1 Inspect the DataFrame
texts.insight: Six columns are float, six are string; the datetimes arrive as text and must be parsed. Sensor columns (latitude, longitude, temperature, humidity, pm2_5, pm10) are float64, which later keeps imputation and scaling straightforward.

texts.title: 1.2 Check for missing values
texts.insight: Missing values are concentrated in the sensor-read columns (573–633 cells), not in site or time metadata. With counts that small relative to 16,374 rows, straightforward imputation is safe.

texts.title: 1.3 Separate numerical and categorical columns
texts.insight: The column split is clean: all 6 numeric columns are candidate features, while of the categoricals only site_name carries predictive information — frequency, network, site_id, and device_name are administrative labels.

texts.title: 1.4 Impute missing values
texts.insight: Mean imputation fills the gaps without changing the row count, letting every row contribute to training. The imputed means sit within plausible ranges, so no synthetic extremes are injected.

texts.title: 1.5 Replace zero sensor readings
texts.insight: Zero-valued temperatures/humidities were sensor failures rather than real readings (0°C or 0% humidity is implausible in Nairobi). Replacing them with site-specific medians removes these spikes while keeping the seasonal profile intact.

texts.title: 1.6 Check for duplicates
texts.insight: Zero duplicate rows means each site-day appears exactly once in the raw data, so no rows were lost to de-duplication and the aggregated daily signal is preserved.

texts.title: 1.7 Convert data types
texts.insight: After parsing, datetime becomes datetime64[us, UTC] — enabling month, day-of-week, and weekend feature extraction — while categorical strings are normalized to lowercase for consistent encoding.

texts.title: 1.8 Drop constant columns
texts.insight: frequency, network, site_id, and device_name are constant or redundant (1 unique value each), so they carry no signal and were dropped. site_name keeps 74 distinct levels and is the only meaningful categorical.

texts.title: 2.1 Inspect categorical variables
texts.insight: site_name is the only categorical feature that matters; its 74 levels are the monitoring sites across Nairobi. The site labels expose meaningful naming differences, which we keep rather than collapsing.

texts.title: 2.2 Split the data into train and test
texts.insight: The 80/20 split holds out ~3,000 site-days for evaluation, so the reported metrics reflect true generalization. Keeping a fixed random_state makes every model comparison reproducible.

texts.title: 2.3 One-hot encode site_name (train/test separately)
texts.insight: One-hot encoding expands site_name to 73 indicator columns on the train set; the test set is reindexed to match so no information leaks between folds. This early encoding is later replaced by a more compact LabelEncoder (site_encoded).

texts.title: 3.0 Summary statistics
texts.insight: A typical Nairobi day reads ~22.7 µg/m³ of PM2.5, right at the boundary between Good (≤12) and Moderate (≤35.4). The spread is large (std ≈ 10.5), meaning many days reach into Unhealthy territory.

texts.title: 3.12 Handling class imbalance with SMOTE
texts.insight: Oversampling rebalances the training classes to 12,755 each so the minority classes are no longer drowned out. SMOTE is applied to the training set only, keeping the test set a faithful measure of real-world performance.

texts.title: 4.1 Datetime decomposition
texts.insight: Decomposing the date exposes day-of-week and weekend signals that the raw datetime string hides. These calendar features feed the model's seasonality component alongside temperature.

texts.title: 4.1.1 Cyclical encoding of date features
texts.insight: Sin/cos encoding keeps month and day-of-week cyclic distances meaningful rather than assigning arbitrary order (e.g., December vs January). This lets the model treat seasonal proximity as similar.

texts.title: 4.2 Site encoding
texts.insight: A numeric site label lets the model treat location as a feature while keeping the input compact compared with one-hot encoding. The 74 codes are assigned by rarity (LabelEncoder order), which is arbitrary but harmless for trees.

texts.title: 4.3 Lagged & rolling features
texts.insight: Yesterday's PM2.5 and the 7-day mean are strong predictors, so historical readings must enter the model. Rolling features were computed per site to avoid mixing one station's history with another's.

texts.title: 4.4 Feature selection
texts.insight: pm10, pm2_5_roll7, and pm2_5_lag1 dominate the correlation ranking — the first three features is the effective core. month_cos (≈ −0.51) confirms seasonality is the strongest exogenous signal.

texts.title: 5.1 Data split (regression + classification targets)
texts.insight: Both tasks share the same 14-feature matrix, but the classification split is stratified so rare classes keep their proportions in train and test. The regression split is plain 80/20; both use random_state=42.

texts.title: 5.2 Feature scaling
texts.insight: Standardizing features to mean 0 / std 1 keeps linear models stable and helps regularization behave consistently. Tree models are unaffected by the scaling but still train on the same transformed matrix for a fair comparison.

texts.title: 5.3.1 Linear Regression
texts.insight: Linear Regression explains ~93% of variance but leaves a bias at the highest PM2.5 values — it systematically under-predicts the most polluted days. Simple and interpretable, it is outclassed on the tail.

texts.title: 5.3.2.1 Tune Ridge alpha (GridSearchCV)
texts.insight: Ridge matches Linear Regression almost exactly — the coefficient estimates are already stable, so added L2 pressure barely moves them. This confirms the linear baselines sit on an easy, smooth error surface.

texts.title: 5.3.3.1 Tune Random Forest Regressor (GridSearchCV)
texts.insight: The Random Forest narrows the error gap noticeably, beating the linear baselines on RMSE while pushing R² toward 0.95. It captures the nonlinear interactions (site × season × history) that a hyperplane cannot.

texts.title: 5.3.3.1 Tune Random Forest Regressor (GridSearchCV)
texts.insight: Tuning highlights that tree depth and feature subsampling matter more than tree count beyond ~200. A shallower forest (max_depth=20) with 75% feature sampling generalizes better than an overgrown one.

texts.title: 5.3.4 Polynomial Regression (degree 2)
texts.insight: Adding an interaction/quadratic layer helps only slightly — most of the gain over linear models comes from the lagged features, not from polynomial flexibility. The pipeline approach also hits scaling limits at degree 2.

texts.title: 5.3.5 Regression models summary & best model
texts.insight: Random Forest wins on every metric; the gap over the linear models confirms the relationship is fundamentally nonlinear. It earns the 'best regressor' slot with R² ≈ 0.95, RMSE ≈ 1.97, MAE ≈ 1.32.

texts.title: 5.4 Classification models comparison
texts.insight: Mapping Good→0, Moderate→1, Unhealthy→2 gives the classifiers a clean numeric target for training while keeping the original labels for reporting. The same encoder is reused across experiments.

texts.title: 5.4.1.1 Tune Logistic Regression (C)
texts.insight: Logistic Regression handles the dominant Moderate class well but struggles to separate the rare classes — its linear boundaries cannot carve out the small Good/Unhealthy regions. Overall accuracy is decent, but recall on minorities suffers.

texts.title: 5.4.1.1 Tune Logistic Regression (C)
texts.insight: Optimal C sits away from the extremes, showing the classifier benefits from some regularization. The best CV accuracy reflects tuning on the balanced objective rather than raw proportions.

texts.title: 5.4.2.1 Tune Random Forest Classifier (GridSearchCV)
texts.insight: Random Forest recovers the rare classes better than Logistic Regression without losing accuracy on Moderate. Non-linear boundaries plus class weighting make it the stronger classifier overall.

texts.title: 5.4.2.1 Tune Random Forest Classifier (GridSearchCV)
texts.insight: The tuned Random Forest is the classification winner, improving recall where Logistic Regression is weakest. Balanced class weights let the forest focus on rare classes without explicit oversampling.

texts.title: 5.4.3 Classification models summary & best model
texts.insight: Random Forest again beats Logistic Regression, mostly by recovering the rare classes while holding ~92% accuracy and macro-F1 ≈ 0.84. Since the task is class-weighted (rare categories matter most), the RF win is the right one.

texts.title: 5.5 Classification with SMOTE-balanced training data
texts.insight: Re-training on SMOTE data lifts the minority-class recall while holding ~92% overall accuracy. The balanced training set also makes precision more uniform across all three categories.

texts.title: 6.3.1 False positives & false negatives analysis
texts.insight: The miss rate is highest for the Unhealthy class — those are the days an air-quality alert would most want to catch. False negatives cluster on transition days (Good→Moderate, Moderate→Unhealthy) where readings sit near a threshold.
